formulas.name: Magnitude of a 2D vector
formulas.explanation: A vector's components are the two short sides of a right-angled triangle, and the vector itself is the hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives its length. The magnitude is never negative, whatever the signs of the components.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the size of a displacement, velocity or force from its components.

example.story: A boat moves 3 units east and 4 units north. How far is it from where it started?

formulas.name: Magnitude of a 3D vector
formulas.explanation: In three dimensions, apply Pythagoras twice: first in the xy plane, then with the z component. The result is the square root of the sum of all three squared components.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the length of any 3D vector, such as a displacement in space or a force with three components.
assumptions: perpendicular x, y and z axes

example.story: Find the length of the vector (2, 3, 6).

formulas.name: Dot product from components
formulas.displayLatex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z

variables.name: a, z component
variables.description: z component of vector a (0 for 2D vectors).

variables.name: b, z component
variables.description: z component of vector b (0 for 2D vectors).

formulas.explanation: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results, giving a single number. It measures how much two vectors point the same way: positive for less than 90 degrees apart, zero for perpendicular, negative for more than 90 degrees. For 2D vectors set the z components to zero.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to test for perpendicular vectors, find angles, compute work (force · displacement), and project one vector onto another.
assumptions: components in the same perpendicular axes

example.story: Find a · b for a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (4, -5, 6).

formulas.name: Dot product from magnitudes and angle

variables.name: angle between
variables.description: The angle between the two vectors, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Geometrically, the dot product is the length of one vector times the length of the other times the cosine of the angle between them. It equals |a| times the part of b that lies along a. This is the same number as the component formula, which is what lets you find angles from components.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know the lengths and the angle, for example work done by a force at an angle to the motion.
assumptions: angle in radians, between 0 and π

example.story: Two vectors of length 3 and 5 make an angle of 60 degrees (π/3). What is their dot product?

formulas.name: Angle between two vectors

variables.name: angle between
variables.description: The angle between the vectors, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Combining the two forms of the dot product gives the cosine of the angle between any two vectors. Compute a · b from components, divide by the product of the lengths, and take acos. It works in any number of dimensions.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the angle between lines, forces, bonds in a molecule, or edges of a 3D shape.
assumptions: neither vector is the zero vector

example.story: Find the angle between a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (4, -5, 6). Their dot product is 12, |a| = √14 and |b| = √77.

formulas.name: Magnitude of the cross product

variables.name: angle between
variables.description: Angle between the vectors, in radians.

formulas.explanation: The cross product of two 3D vectors is a vector perpendicular to both, with direction given by the right-hand rule. Its length equals the area of the parallelogram the two vectors span, which is |a||b| sin θ. Parallel vectors have a zero cross product.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for areas of parallelograms and triangles in 3D, torque (r × F), and magnetic forces (q v × B).

example.story: Vectors of length 2 and 3 make an angle of 30 degrees. What is the area of the parallelogram they span?

formulas.name: Cross product component
formulas.displayLatex: (\vec a \times \vec b)_z = a_x b_y - a_y b_x

variables.name: z component of a × b
variables.description: The component of the cross product along z.

formulas.explanation: Each component of a × b uses the other two components of a and b. The z component is a_x b_y - a_y b_x; the x and y components follow the cyclic pattern: c_x = a_y b_z - a_z b_y and c_y = a_z b_x - a_x b_z. For two vectors in the xy plane, c_z is the signed area of their parallelogram: positive if b is anticlockwise from a.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compute cross products from components, or to tell whether a turn is clockwise or anticlockwise in 2D.

example.story: Find the z component of a × b for a = (3, 1, 0) and b = (2, 4, 0).

formulas.name: Determinant of a 2x2 matrix
formulas.displayLatex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc
formulas.explanation: The determinant is the factor by which the matrix scales areas, with a negative sign if it flips orientation. It is the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal. A determinant of zero means the matrix squashes the plane onto a line and has no inverse.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to check whether a matrix is invertible, to solve 2x2 linear systems (Cramer's rule), or to find area scale factors.

example.story: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows (3, 8) and (4, 6).

formulas.name: Determinant of a 3x3 matrix
formulas.explanation: Expand along the first row: each entry multiplies the 2x2 determinant left when you cross out its row and column, with signs alternating +, -, +. The result is the volume scale factor of the matrix. A zero determinant means the three rows (or columns) lie in one plane.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to test whether a 3x3 system has a unique solution, for volumes of parallelepipeds, and in the scalar triple product.

example.story: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows (2, -3, 1), (2, 0, -1) and (1, 4, 5).

formulas.name: Inverse of a 2x2 matrix
formulas.displayLatex: \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}

variables.name: top-left entry of the inverse
variables.description: The entry in row 1, column 1 of the inverse matrix.

variables.name: bottom-right entry
variables.description: Row 2, column 2 of the original matrix.

variables.name: top-left entry
variables.description: Row 1, column 1 of the original matrix.

variables.name: top-right entry
variables.description: Row 1, column 2 of the original matrix.

variables.name: bottom-left entry
variables.description: Row 2, column 1 of the original matrix.

formulas.explanation: To invert a 2x2 matrix, swap the two diagonal entries, change the sign of the other two, and divide everything by the determinant ad - bc. The equation gives the top-left entry d/(ad - bc); the others are -b/(ad - bc), -c/(ad - bc) and a/(ad - bc). Multiplying the matrix by its inverse gives the identity matrix.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations written as a matrix equation, or to undo a 2D transformation.
assumptions: ad - bc ≠ 0 (otherwise there is no inverse)

example.story: Find the top-left entry of the inverse of the matrix with rows (4, 7) and (2, 6).

formulas.name: Scalar projection of one vector onto another

variables.name: scalar projection
variables.description: Signed length of the shadow of a on the direction of b.

variables.name: magnitude of b
variables.description: Length of the vector projected onto.

formulas.explanation: The scalar projection is how far vector a reaches along the direction of b, like the length of its shadow when light shines perpendicular to b. It equals |a| cos θ, which is a · b divided by |b|. Multiplying it by the unit vector b/|b| gives the vector projection.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the component of a force along a slope, or the part of a velocity in a given direction.
assumptions: b is not the zero vector

example.story: How far does a = (2, 3) reach along the direction of b = (4, 0)? Here a · b = 8 and |b| = 4.

formulas.name: Unit vector

variables.name: unit vector component
variables.description: One component of the unit vector in the direction of v.

formulas.explanation: A unit vector has length 1 and shows only a direction. Dividing every component of v by its length shrinks or stretches it to length 1 without turning it. Apply the equation to each component in turn.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to describe a direction on its own, for example the direction of a force, or before projecting onto a direction.
assumptions: v is not the zero vector

example.story: Find the x component of the unit vector in the direction of (3, 4), which has length 5.

formulas.name: Direction angle of a 2D vector

variables.name: direction angle
variables.description: Angle from the positive x axis, in radians.

formulas.explanation: The components form a right-angled triangle with the vector, so the tangent of its angle to the x axis is v_y over v_x. Calculators return an angle between -90 and 90 degrees, so check the quadrant: if v_x is negative, add 180 degrees (π).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to give the direction of a velocity, force or displacement from its components, for example a bearing.
assumptions: check the quadrant from the signs of the components

example.story: A velocity has components (2, 2). What angle does it make with the x axis?

formulas.name: Distance between two points in 3D

variables.name: x of second point
variables.description: x coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: x of first point
variables.description: x coordinate of the first point.

variables.name: y of second point
variables.description: y coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: y of first point
variables.description: y coordinate of the first point.

variables.name: z of second point
variables.description: z coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: z of first point
variables.description: z coordinate of the first point.

formulas.explanation: The distance between two points is the magnitude of the vector from one to the other. Subtract matching coordinates, square, add and take the square root, just like the 2D formula with an extra term.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for distances in 3D geometry, between atoms in a molecule, or between positions in space.

example.story: How far apart are the points (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 15)?

formulas.name: Resultant of two vectors at an angle

variables.name: first vector
variables.description: Size of the first force or vector.

variables.name: second vector
variables.description: Size of the second force or vector.

variables.name: angle between
variables.description: Angle between the two vectors when placed tail to tail, in radians.

formulas.explanation: Adding two vectors tip to tail forms a triangle, and the cosine rule gives the length of the third side. With θ measured between the vectors placed tail to tail, the sign in front of the cosine term is plus. At θ = 0 the sizes simply add; at θ = π they subtract.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to combine two forces or velocities acting at an angle, such as a boat crossing a current.
assumptions: θ is the angle between the vectors placed tail to tail

example.story: Two ropes pull a crate with forces of 3 N and 4 N at 60 degrees to each other. What is the size of the resultant force?

formulas.name: Eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix

variables.name: eigenvalue
variables.description: A number with A v = λ v for some non-zero vector v.

variables.name: trace
variables.description: Sum of the diagonal entries, a + d.

formulas.explanation: An eigenvector is only stretched by the matrix, not turned, and the stretch factor is its eigenvalue. The condition det(A - λI) = 0 for a 2x2 matrix becomes this quadratic, the characteristic equation. Its two roots add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix in systems of differential equations, vibrations, Markov chains or principal axes.

example.story: Find an eigenvalue of the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2). Its trace is 4 and its determinant is 3.
